candidate.educational_objective: Use systems-based workplace-violence prevention in healthcare: identify hazards, train staff, support reporting, and apply staffing, environmental, and security controls rather than relying on individual workers.

options.A: Use a workplace-violence prevention program with worksite hazard analysis, de-escalation training, reporting, security/environmental controls, and measures that reduce isolated work when feasible.
options.B: Ask staff not to report threats that do not cause injury because documenting lower-level events increases administrative workload without improving prevention.
options.C: Rely mainly on individual staff confidence because formal training, environmental design, security planning, and staffing practices do not materially affect violence risk.
options.D: Encourage staff to approach escalating visitors alone so other patients are not alarmed and security is used only after an actual physical assault occurs.

candidate.rationale: OSHA identifies working alone, poor environmental design, inadequate security, and lack of training/policies as healthcare workplace-violence risk factors. Recognized controls include a workplace-violence prevention program with management commitment, employee participation, worksite analysis, hazard prevention/control, training, recordkeeping, and program evaluation; OSHA also describes de-escalation and reporting practices. A is therefore the best systems-based response.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Healthcare workplace-violence risk is addressed through a comprehensive prevention program, hazard analysis, training, reporting, and engineering/administrative/security controls.
